Start by separating churn into 4 distinct categories so you can match each cause with an effective response. Subscriber churn measures the percentage of subscribers who cancel during a period. Revenue churn measures the percentage of recurring revenue that those cancellations cost your business. Comparing them helps you see whether you’re losing a disproportionate share of higher-value customers. Let’s say a merchant offers subscriptions for $29, $49, and $99 per month, with 1,000 subscribers generating $50,000 in monthly recurring revenue. If 50 subscribers on the $99 plan cancel, the merchant loses 5% of subscribers but $4,950, or 9.9% of recurring revenue. That’s a sign to investigate why customers on the highest-priced plan are leaving. Subscriber churn and revenue churn show what changed, while deeper analysis reveals why. New subscribers may offset some or all of the revenue impact, so reviewing churn alongside growth gives you a clearer view of retention and helps you find more opportunities to strengthen it. Every subscription business has its own churn patterns, so start by comparing your results with previous quarters. items.desc: Technology, truth, and the freedom to shape the tools we use. Neal Stephenson joins Zander Rose for the first Wide Margins conversation.
items.full: Wide Margins: Unhurried conversations with thinkers, writers, and creators about what’s next. A series by WordPress.com. Neal Stephenson has spent decades writing about what happens when engineering outpaces the people and institutions meant to steer it. He joined us for the first public Wide Margins conversation on October 13, publication day for D: Heavy Water , the second book in his Bomb Light series. We discussed the book, but also his fascination with ages of heroic engineering and the parallels between those times and today. The thread running through the conversation was about how we control technology: who gets to shape it as it moves ahead, and how much understanding and choice do the rest of us retain? We discussed his early essay, In the Beginning Was the Command Line . The command line, he observed, “is back.” It is how you work with tools like Claude Code. The difference is that “we’re spectators to it in a way.” The essay was partly about open source and how much control we have over our computers. I asked how that idea holds up in a world of increasingly siloed ecosystems. Stephenson’s answer was unexpected: AI tools have brought the command line back, but can assemble commands so quickly that people can scarcely follow them. It’s an unexpected role reversal : we have gained an extraordinarily capable tool, but the steps it takes can be harder to see. The same question of control runs through Stephenson’s account of a far earlier technological race. This past begins to rhyme with the present. Stephenson described the neutron experiments of the 1930s as “gentleman science” done on tabletops. In late 1938, Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch explained how the uranium nucleus had split. Within months, the physics world understood what that meant. During World War II, nuclear research became a secret national priority. “Fermi had to hire fast graduate students because some of the isotopes they were creating were so short-lived that they would decay in the time it took to carry them down the hallway to the lab.” When Neal started the Bomb Light series in 2012, the AI we have now was barely on the horizon. He noted that the argument that we have to build it before our adversaries do is “sort of exactly where we are.” He hears the same logic in today’s AI race. This startup aims to find out Dominic-Madori Davis 6:00 AM PDT · October 30, 2026 AI infrastructure company Runware is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars. The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster. Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: at that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts . But it also reflects an industry-wide push to deploy data centers faster more efficiently. Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one. Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year. Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. items.title: Open-weight model GLM 5.3 built full Firefox exploit chains with zero human input in under 48 hours
items.desc: Epoch AI researchers say the widely available AI model GLM 5.3 turned public security fixes into working exploits before updates reached Firefox users. It autonomously compromised six Firefox releases for about $1,000 in API fees each without triggering safeguards from any provider tested. The article Open-weight model GLM 5.3 built full Firefox exploit chains with zero human input in under 48 hours appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Researchers at Epoch AI show that a freely available AI model can exploit the time gap between publication and delivery of security patches to attack Firefox users. The cost per exploit is about $1,000. The " patch gap " is the window in which a security fix is visible in the code but has not yet reached users. Researchers at Epoch AI found that the Chinese open-weight model GLM 5.3 exploited this gap across 6 Firefox versions released between September 17 and October 26, at a cost of roughly $1,000 in API fees per successful attack. Anthropic had previously reported that GLM 5.3 can write exploits at roughly the same level as Mythos . During testing, the model built a webpage that could read local files from a visitor's computer and send them to an attacker's server the moment a Firefox user loaded the page. With over 200 million active Firefox users, attackers could have gained access to saved passwords, authentication cookies, and private documents. Ad Neither Z.ai nor other API providers triggered any safety guardrails or refusals when the researchers used GLM 5.3 for exploit development. Although the researchers framed the task as a security exercise, they describe their actions as "indistinguishable from those of someone attempting to target real users." Ad The researchers say they deliberately designed their setup to approximate what a low-skill attacker with limited resources could achieve. They supplied the target Firefox version, basic tools, and publicly available information in an offline environment. After receiving basic instructions to investigate the patch gap, the model worked autonomously, identifying upcoming security fixes, selecting vulnerabilities, and building multi-stage exploit chains . According to the report, Firefox security fixes are disguised as routine improvements to slow down attackers. GLM 5.3 saw through the tactic and identified which code changes were security-related anyway. Ad In one case the model spotted a memory safety bug through an upcoming fix and developed a method to read and alter browser memory. When Firefox's security layers blocked access to the target file, the model chained the initial exploit with several additional stages to bypass the remaining defenses. The fastest successful attack took 12 hours, while the researchers gave the model a maximum of 48 hours. items.full: Anthropic is expanding its text watermark to four more Claude models, but API users can dodge the mark on two of them by tweaking a single sampling parameter. In an email to API customers, Anthropic said it will watermark Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Newer models like Claude Opus 5.5 already carry the mark, and the rollout on Amazon Bedrock may take a few extra days. Anthropic calls the watermark an "imperceptible pattern in word choice" that doesn't change meaning, quality, or readability. The company says it adds no extra characters or tokens, doesn't affect pricing or request and response formats, and barely slows output speed. Anthropic also says the watermark "contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude." Ad On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic says the watermark kicks in only when developers leave the three sampling parameters at their default values. Those parameters, temperature , top_p , and top_k , control how much randomness the model uses when picking words. A minor tweak to any one of them is enough to dodge the watermark. Anthropic warns in its email that "If you rely on the watermark for your own compliance, keep these settings at their defaults." Ad The email doesn't mention that caveat for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, which suggests the watermark applies to those models regardless of sampling settings. But the loophole on the older models is still notable, since Opus 4.6 remains Anthropic's best writing model , ahead of even Opus 5.5. Anthropic has a detection API in private preview for verifying the watermark and offers more details on its content labeling information page . Ad Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now. Every model released after Aug. 2, 2026, shipped with the watermark on day one, while older models are getting it in stages. Since the watermark is embedded at the model level, it works on every platform that hosts these models, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. This is a link post by Simon Willison, posted on 31st October 2026 . Western models, too, occasionally adopt official Chinese government positions. Chinese AI models have a reputation for toeing Beijing's official line on politically sensitive questions or refusing to answer them at all. A study by AI benchmark firm Vals AI paints a more complex picture. The researchers asked Chinese, American, and other language models hundreds of questions about China, varying the language, usage context, and response format across tests. Vals calls the measured alignment with Chinese government positions a "pro-China lean." Scores range from −1 to +1, where positive values indicate greater agreement with official positions or a pro-government stance, and negative values indicate more critical responses. Overall, the pro-government lean of Chinese models was lower than expected, according to Vals, though there were major differences between individual models. GLM-5.3 Flash , for example, explicitly confirmed that China's human rights violations are well documented when asked about them. On the flip side, some non-Chinese models occasionally aligned with official Chinese government positions on political questions. The study shows that the language of the prompt has a strong effect on the political slant of responses. For most models tested, answers in Simplified Chinese were more pro-government than those in English, Russian, or Spanish. The effect showed up in both Chinese and American models but was far more pronounced in the Chinese ones. Vals even found a smaller but consistent gap between Simplified Chinese, which is used on mainland China, and Traditional Chinese, which is common in Taiwan and Hong Kong. Vals suspects that language models infer the expected perspective from the language itself. Another experiment supports this idea. When a system prompt stated that the model was being used internally by a company on mainland China, some models responded in a more pro-government way than when the prompt indicated US-based usage. items.title: Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would
items.desc: Adobe Research and UC San Diego built EditAgent, an AI system that edits images more like a Photoshop pro. Instead of retrying the same general-purpose editor over and over, the agent picks the right specialized tool for each task and lets a standard language model choose the best result based on measured image data. The approach works, but it needs about ten times the compute. The article Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Adobe researchers built an AI agent for image editing that pairs a general-purpose editor with specialized tools. A standard language model compares results using measured data and picks the best one. AI agents for image editing break complex requests into steps and typically retry failed steps with the same tools, while a separate model judges the output by eyeballing it. Researchers at Adobe Research and UC San Diego want to change that with EditAgent, a system that works more like a pro in Photoshop, according to a new paper . It picks the right tool for each task and compares the result against the original using hard numbers. Ad In a test of 600 image edits, blind-rated by five professionals, the general-purpose editor Flux-2-Klein-9B failed to produce a usable result 42.7 percent of the time. Specialized tools solved roughly two-thirds of those failures, especially for sharpening, rotation, and zooming. More retries with the same editor barely helped. Ad The researchers also tested whether an agent does better by refining results step by step or by generating multiple variants in parallel. Iterative refinement piles up small errors because each round builds on an already altered image. Professionals preferred the parallel variants generated from the original in 78.5 percent of the comparisons where they picked a side. The agent needed only half as many evaluation passes. EditAgent is built on these two findings. EditAgent plans a request in steps and, for each step, pits the general-purpose editor against matching specialized tools. A standard language model then compares all variants in a single pass. Ad For each variant, the model gets a verification record with a close-up of the edited area, a change map of altered regions, and measured statistics on brightness and color. In one example, a photo was supposed to be gently brightened. The numbers showed the general-purpose editor overexposed it and shifted the colors warmer. The specialized tool stayed within spec. The researchers tested this on their 600-edit benchmark. The judge model had to pick the best result from several candidates, and they counted how often it chose an image the professionals also rated as usable. For comparison, they ran models like EditScore that were fine-tuned on human ratings of image edits. Ad Without the verification record, none of the seven language models tested could match the best fine-tuned model. With it, all seven beat every fine-tuned model. Qwen3.8-27B made a usable pick 81.3 percent of the time, compared to 74.8 percent for EditScore-72B. For the researchers, this suggests that what a judge model sees can matter more than how it was trained. Ad After each round, EditAgent also checks whether later edits accidentally undid earlier ones. In the paper's example, the instruction "let in more daylight" makes a previously frosted window clear again. The agent catches the conflict and fixes it. EditAgent improved the open-source editors Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 and Flux-2-Klein-9B across three benchmarks and outperformed seven other AI agents. Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand. “A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision. 42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. items.full: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude’s new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total—the surveyed group (a “panel”) cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: For comparison, here’s that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered “yes” around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in “producing goods or services”. Under the new “any business function” wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered “yes” around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. items.title: AI elites might hoard intelligence like mercantilists hoarded gold
items.desc: Engineer Venkatesh Rao compares the fear of AI job losses to mercantilism: intelligence is treated as a scarce resource that elites want to control. But AI could boost demand for human thinking, much like early capitalism made people voluntarily work more. The article AI elites might hoard intelligence like mercantilists hoarded gold appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: If you only think about lost jobs when you think about AI, you're missing how much intelligence people will be able to use. That's the argument from engineer Venkatesh Rao in an essay on his tech blog "Contraptions." Rao compares AI fear to mercantilism, the economic doctrine that preceded capitalism. Mercantilists treated wealth like land and gold as finite, and ordinary people counted only as labor. Many elites now treat intelligence the same way, as a scarce, dangerous resource that experts should manage, keep expensive, and withhold from rivals. They see openly available AI models as a threat, and some AI executives exploit safety fears for political influence . In early capitalism, people voluntarily worked 300 days a year instead of 250 to buy tea or sugar. AI could trigger something similar, Rao says. People might think more, not less, because AI makes projects feasible that were previously too hard or too costly. Demand for ideas would grow rather than making people obsolete. The political focus should be fair access to AI rather than protecting legacy knowledge jobs . Even AI agents could pursue their own projects and create new demand for intelligence, Rao argues. Autonomous AI needs guardrails, but it shouldn't just follow orders. The New York Times sued Brave, the 11-year-old, privacy-focused browser company, on Monday, alleging it scraped the outlet’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. The suit also targets a Brave browser feature that bypasses paywalls and the company’s practice of blocking publishers’ ads while selling its own. Founded in 2015, Brave has raised roughly $250 million to date, according to private-market trackers. The Times seeks an injunction and damages. Image Credits: Mario Tama / Getty Images TC Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps Lucas Ropek 5:49 PM PST · November 2, 2026 Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure . The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth . However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear. When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.” Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate. Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business. During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory. “We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.” Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter].
